hints.title: Key Insight and Observation
hints.text: The first array is constrained to a tiny size of at most five elements.

hints.title: Algorithmic Strategy and State
hints.text: A type 2 query checks how many elements in the second array equal tot minus nums1[j].

hints.title: Optimal Boundary and Processing
hints.text: Update the second array directly on range increments and sum target frequencies.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```python
from collections import Counter

def numberOfPairs(nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int], queries: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
    n2 = nums2[:]
    ans = []
    freq = Counter(n2)
    for q in queries:
        if q[0] == 1:
            _, l, r, val = q
            for i in range(l, r + 1):
                old = n2[i]
                freq[old] -= 1
                n2[i] += val
                freq[n2[i]] += 1
        else:
            _, tot = q
            total_pairs = 0
            for x in nums1:
                target = tot - x
                total_pairs += freq[target]
            ans.append(total_pairs)
    return ans
```

complexity.notes: Small size of nums1 enables constant time frequency queries per target total.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Nested loop pair counts per query take O(q * n1 * n2).
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Frequency mapping tracks counts of second array elements.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Leverages constraint that nums1 size is at most 5.
